source.title: Rethinking Bias-Variance Trade-off for Generalization of Neural Networks
source.authors: Zi-Tong Yang; Yaodong Yu; Chong You; Jacob Steinhardt; Yi Ma

record.tranche_reason: The study measures risk across network widths and reports that the curve is usually monotone decreasing, becomes unimodal under one loss, and shows double descent with added label noise. It refines the generality of double descent rather than reproducing the original experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports measurements of risk and train/test error over width, and measurements of bias and variance. It does not sweep training epochs or use training sample size as the curve axis for the more-data claim. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study measures test risk across network width for several deep networks and a two-layer linear random-feature model. It argues that double descent is one special case of monotone bias plus unimodal variance, seen mainly with label noise. Clean-label curves are usually monotone decreasing. This is a specific argument that V1 needs restating, so T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Bias decreases with width while variance is unimodal, and their sum yields monotone, double-descent or unimodal risk. Monotone decreasing risk is the most common case because bias dominates. Double descent appears when label noise inflates variance; the authors frame it as a special case explained by classical bias-variance analysis.
record.recipe_differences: The study estimates random-design bias and variance from independent data splits and measures risk across widths, architectures, losses, datasets, and label-noise conditions. It does not reproduce the original epoch-wise or sample-wise sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The risk shape depends on loss and label-noise conditions: clean MSE risk is reported as monotone decreasing, cross-entropy risk as unimodal, and added label noise produces double descent.

fits_no_version.finding: Across all architectures, datasets and losses tested, variance is unimodal in width and bias is monotonically decreasing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-design variance of neural networks is unimodal in width, while bias decreases monotonically.

fits_no_version.finding: In the two-layer linear model, the variance peak falls at p≈d/2−λ0·d; this is confirmed in a synthetic experiment (Fig 22).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The variance peak location is set by input dimension rather than by the interpolation threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Deeper ResNets and VGGs have lower bias and higher variance. The out-of-distribution (CIFAR10-C) accuracy drop comes mostly from increased bias.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Depth trades bias for variance, and out-of-distribution error is bias-dominated.

record.problems: The cross-entropy variance estimator is not unbiased; the authors report that it overestimates bias and underestimates variance at small numbers of splits. The key curves are mainly presented in figures, and the text does not give numeric peak locations or establish their alignment with interpolation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were needed for the reported width-risk outcomes. Results on bias and variance alone, depth comparisons, and OOD evaluation were left out where they do not measure a version's named risk curve. The sample-size comparisons do not test whether more data hurts near interpolation.

untested.parts: Whether the risk peak, when present, sits at the width where training error first reaches zero.
All of it; there is no sweep over epochs.
Whether more samples hurt near the interpolation threshold. The paper only notes that 2,500 vs 10,000 samples raises bias and variance.
Non-neural model classes beyond the linear random-feature model, and whether the classical U-shape is subsumed.
All of it. The predicted p≈d/2 peak is for variance, not for a risk peak predicted by effective complexity.
Multiple or split peaks, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak. Only two weight-decay values are compared, and only for variance.
All of it; no effective-parameter recounting.

missing.what: Clean-label risk-vs-width curves for other architectures, which the text calls monotone decreasing: ResNext29 (CIFAR10), MLP on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, VGG11 and CIFAR100 ResNet34.
Clean ResNet34 risk at 10,000 and 2,500 training samples; Fig 12 is the 0% baseline for Fig 4/15.
Weight decay 1e-4 vs 5e-4: larger weight decay lowers variance.
Risk curves for 0%, 10% and 20% label noise plotted together.

record.verdict_notes: R1 changed from reversed to absent. V4 links removed from deep-net rows to avoid duplicating V1 verdicts. V4 rests only on R5, which works in a regime (large n/d) far from interpolation. Figures carry no numeric peak locations.

versions.untested_parts: The text does not state that the peak, when present, is precisely aligned with the size at which the model just fits the training set.
No risk sweep over training epochs is reported.
The study compares results at different training-set sizes but does not test whether adding samples raises test error near an interpolation threshold.
The experiments cover several neural-network settings and a two-layer linear model, not model classes generally; the precise relation to capacity past interpolation is not established.
The study does not test a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The study varies label noise and reports a comparison of weight-decay settings, but does not test multiple or split peaks or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The study does not test whether counting effective parameters turns a second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: two-layer linear network with random Gaussian first layer
rows.size_stated: hidden-unit count p; asymptotic width ratio γ = p/d
rows.stage_stated: ridge regression estimates the second-layer parameters
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed risk as width and the sample-to-dimension ratio vary.
rows.value: The plotted risk changes from unimodal to monotonically decreasing as the number of samples increases.
rows.note: This is a theoretical two-layer linear model; the result does not establish a universal curve across model classes.
rows.check: This is a two-layer linear random-feature ridge model; only the n/d→∞ case is analytic, and the other n/d values are plotted. Risk is unimodal at small n/d and monotone decreasing at large n/d, never a full fall-rise-fall curve. Subject should say ridge-regularized random-feature model.
